definition.text: A kind of negotiation in which a buyer and a seller argue over the price or terms of a deal.

facts.text: If the two sides agree on terms, the trade goes ahead.
Bargaining has largely disappeared where fixed-price shops dominate, but remains common for expensive goods such as homes, cars and jewellery.
Emotions, mental biases and a sense of fairness strongly affect bargaining; the endowment effect makes sellers ask more than buyers will pay.
Coase argued that without transaction costs, people would bargain their way to the same use of resources however a court ruled in a property dispute.

definition.text: John Nash's answer to how two parties should split the gains from agreeing: the deal that maximizes the product of what each gains over failing to agree.

facts.text: Nash (1950) defined a bargaining problem as the set of possible agreements plus a disagreement point, what each gets if talks fail.
Bargaining solutions are usually built from axioms such as efficiency, symmetry and independence of irrelevant alternatives.
The Nash solution handles only the simplest structure and does not show how efficient outcomes are reached over time.

definition.text: A way of picturing property ownership as a set of separate rights, like sticks in a bundle, that can be split among different people and put back together.

facts.text: The idea began with Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld in 1913, though he never used the phrase.
The five traditional rights are possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment (use, including resource extraction) and disposition (transfer).
Parts of a right can be held separately: a tenant may live on land while someone else owns the minerals or water beneath it.
Governments keep rights such as environmental regulation, zoning and eminent domain, and third parties may hold rights such as conservation easements.

title: Common good (economics)

definition.text: In economics, a good that is rival (one person's use leaves less for others) but non-excludable (people cannot be kept from using it).

facts.text: Because anyone can use them, common goods risk being overexploited when people act in their own interest.
A road is a public good when empty, but once congested each extra driver slows others, turning it into a common good.
Fish stocks in international waters, among the least regulated common resources, are likely to be depleted if fish are taken without limits.
Aristotle already observed that 'what is common to many is taken least care of'.

notes: The page calls common goods a synonym of common-pool resources, while 'Common-pool resource' and S:f8082e4ff72b reserve that term for institutionally managed commons; ordering pass may fold this into 'Common-pool resource'. Section 'Common goods and normal goods' (S:33a65d90d75b, S:37c13835fbbf) is confused and was not used.

definition.text: A usually unpriced good from nature or green infrastructure, such as clean air and water, landscapes, parks, rivers, forests and beaches.

facts.text: Environmental goods are a sub-category of public goods.
They are hard to protect because users pay nothing up front and pollution can damage them indefinitely.
There is no agreed method for putting an economic value on them; obstacles include free riding, unclear ownership and the fact that they cannot be divided up.
Economists try to value them by asking people's willingness to pay, sometimes with simulated markets and contingent valuation, but critics cite framing effects and biases.
Alternative measures of progress, such as the Genuine Progress Indicator and Gross National Happiness, count environmental damage and resource depletion.

title: Environmental Goods Agreement

definition.text: Talks among 18 World Trade Organization members, begun in 2015, to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment.

facts.text: In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means products used to protect the environment, such as renewable energy technology and pollution control systems.
The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, renewable energy, monitoring and energy efficiency.
The negotiations collapsed in 2016.

notes: Uses a different sense of 'environmental good' (traded green technologies); may belong in a trade chapter.
